title: How Do Planes Fly?
summary: Wings make lift by turning moving air downward; pressure and Newton's third law are two views of the same thing.
objectives: Explain lift as **air turned downward** by a moving wing
Connect the **pressure** view and the **Newton** view of lift
Use the **lift equation** to predict what doubling speed or area does
Explain what **angle of attack** does and why wings **stall**
Spot the **equal transit time** myth and say why it's wrong

steps.title: A wing sitting in moving air

state.caption: Air streams past a wing, like a hand out of a car window

steps.narration: Hold your flat hand out of a moving car's window and you feel the air push on it. A wing is a carefully shaped hand. Lift needs a solid body **moving relative to air** [S1].

steps.title: Tilt it up a little

state.caption: Tilt the front up and the wing rises

steps.narration: Tilt the front of your hand up and it gets pushed up. Pilots call that tilt the **angle of attack**. A little more angle makes a lot more lift [S3].

steps.title: Air goes down, wing goes up

state.caption: Push air down and the air pushes you up

steps.narration: Watch the blue dots behind the wing: they get **turned downward**. Pushing air down means the air pushes the wing up, just like a swimmer pushing water back to move forward [S1].
whatChanged: + air leaving the wing points down

steps.title: No air, no lift
steps.narration: Take the air away and the wing has nothing to push on. That's why the Space Shuttle's wings didn't hold it up in space: **no fluid, no lift** [S1].

steps.title: Too much tilt: stall

state.caption: Tilt too far and the air stops following the wing

steps.narration: Tilt your hand too steeply and the air can't follow the top surface any more. It breaks away in swirls and the lift suddenly drops. That's a **stall** [S3].

callout.text: A stall is about the wing's angle to the air, not the engine stopping.

whatChanged: - smooth flow on top breaks up

steps.title: Meet the wing
steps.narration: This is a wing section: rounded at the front, thin at the back, slightly curved. Drag the view to look around. Most of an airliner's lift comes from its wings [S1].

steps.title: Turn on the air
steps.narration: Now air streams past from left to right. It makes no difference whether the wing moves through still air or air moves past a still wing; only the **relative motion** matters [S1].

steps.title: Tilt: angle of attack
steps.narration: The angle between the wing's chord line and the oncoming air is the **angle of attack**. At takeoff the pilot 'rotates' the plane, raising the nose to increase it [S3].

steps.title: The air is turned down
steps.narration: Follow the streamlines: air rises slightly ahead of the wing and leaves **angled downward** behind it. Both the upper and lower surfaces help turn it [S1].

callout.text: Ignoring the upper surface's part in turning the flow leads to a wrong theory of lift [S1].

steps.title: Newton: turned air pushes back
steps.narration: Turn a flow one way and you get a force the other way: Newton's third law. Air pushed **down** means the wing is pushed **up** [S1]. When lift matches weight, the plane holds its height.

steps.title: Bernoulli: low pressure on top
steps.narration: Air over the top moves **faster** (watch the dots) and its pressure drops (blue). Below, pressure is higher (red). Adding up the pressure all around the wing gives the same force [S4].

callout.text: Pressure and flow turning aren't rival theories; they're two ways of adding up one force [S4].

steps.title: Faster means much more lift
steps.narration: Lift depends on the **square** of speed [S2]. At 1.6× the speed the wing makes about 2.5× the lift. That's why planes need long runways to build speed before liftoff.

steps.title: Too steep: the stall
steps.narration: Past roughly 15° here, the air **separates** from the upper surface and swirls. The wing suddenly loses lift: a **stall** [S3]. Predicting the exact stall angle is hard, so engineers measure it in wind tunnels [S3].

callout.text: Recovering from a stall means lowering the nose to reduce the angle of attack.

steps.title: Four forces
steps.narration: Lift directly opposes the airplane's **weight** [S1]. Thrust pushes it forward and drag resists the motion. In steady level flight, lift balances weight and thrust balances drag.

steps.title: Lift is perpendicular to the flow
steps.narration: Lift is defined as the part of the aerodynamic force **perpendicular** to the oncoming flow; drag is the part **parallel** to it [S1]. Lift acts through the **center of pressure** [S1].

callout.text: 'Perpendicular to the flow' isn't always 'up': on a banked turn, lift tilts with the wings.

steps.title: The lift equation

state.caption: Every factor that matters, in one line

steps.narration: Lift equals the **lift coefficient** times **density** times **half the velocity squared** times **wing area** [S2]. The coefficient Cl bundles the hard parts: shape, angle, viscosity and compressibility [S2].

steps.title: Dynamic pressure links to Bernoulli
steps.narration: The group ρV²/2 is the **dynamic pressure**, the same term in Bernoulli's equation [S2]. Bernoulli says static pressure plus dynamic pressure stays constant along the flow [S5]: speed up the air and its static pressure falls.

steps.title: Cl rises with angle, then stalls

state.caption: Lift coefficient vs angle of attack (typical thin airfoil)

steps.narration: For thin airfoils, lift is **directly proportional** to angle of attack for small angles, within about ±10° [S3]. Beyond that the curve bends, and past the stall point the flow becomes unsteady [S3].

steps.title: Why camber matters
steps.narration: A curved (**cambered**) airfoil makes a little lift even at zero angle. A **symmetric** airfoil makes zero lift at zero angle [S3], which is why aerobatic planes, which fly upside down, often use symmetric wings.

steps.title: Air sticks to the surface
steps.narration: Air molecules **stick** to the wing's surface, creating a thin **boundary layer** that, in effect, changes the wing's shape. The flow turning responds to the edge of that layer, not the bare metal [S3].

steps.title: The layer separates
steps.narration: At high angles the boundary layer can **lift off**, or separate, from the body. The effective shape becomes very different from the real one, and the wing abruptly loses lift [S3].

steps.title: Why the stall angle is measured, not computed
steps.narration: Predicting the stall point mathematically is very difficult, so engineers rely on **wind-tunnel tests** that carefully match the real aircraft's similarity parameters [S3]. Past stall, lift varies rapidly with time, so plots usually stop there [S3].

steps.title: Double the speed
steps.narration: Velocity is **squared** in the lift equation [S2], so doubling speed quadruples lift. Halving speed cuts lift to a quarter, which is why landing approaches need high-lift flaps.

steps.title: Double the wing area
steps.narration: Area enters **linearly** [S2]: twice the wing area gives twice the lift at the same speed and angle. Big, slow aircraft such as gliders lean on large wing areas.

steps.title: Thinner air
steps.narration: Lift is proportional to air **density** ρ [S2]. Halve the density, as in thin high-altitude air, and you halve the lift unless you fly faster or at a higher angle to make up for it.

tabs.title: Story & Misconceptions
tabs.intro: Two centuries of physics came before anyone flew; the names Bernoulli and Newton got attached to lift much later.

timeline.title: Newton's laws of motion
timeline.text: Isaac Newton presents his three laws of motion in the *Principia* [S4]. The third, action and reaction, later explains flow turning.

timeline.title: Bernoulli's Hydrodynamica
timeline.text: Daniel Bernoulli applies conservation of energy to fluid flow [S4]. Neither he nor Newton ever tried to explain aerodynamic lift [S4].

timeline.title: Cayley's fixed-wing idea
timeline.text: George Cayley sets out the modern aeroplane: a fixed wing with separate systems for lift, propulsion and control [S6].

timeline.title: A glider carries a person
timeline.text: A larger Cayley glider flies across Brompton Dale; Cayley designed the first glider reliably reported to carry a human aloft [S6].

timeline.title: Lilienthal's gliding flights
timeline.text: Otto Lilienthal makes the first well-documented, repeated, successful glider flights [S7]. In 1896 his glider stalls and he dies of his injuries [S7].

timeline.title: First powered, controlled flight
timeline.text: On 17 December the Wright brothers' Flyer makes the first sustained flight of a manned, powered, controlled heavier-than-air aircraft [S8].

misconceptions.myth: Air over the longer top surface must 'meet up' with air underneath at the trailing edge, so it speeds up (**equal transit time**).
misconceptions.why: Nothing forces the two parcels to meet. Real flow over the top of a lifting wing is **much faster** than equal transit would predict [S4].
misconceptions.truth: Use the real velocity distribution; Bernoulli then gives the right pressure, and the pressure gives the right force [S4].

misconceptions.myth: Lift is air bouncing off the wing's **underside**, like a stone skipping on water.
misconceptions.why: It ignores the upper surface, which also turns the flow [S4].
misconceptions.truth: Both the upper and lower surfaces turn the flow downward, and both contribute to lift [S1].

misconceptions.myth: The top of a wing is half of a **Venturi nozzle** that squeezes the air faster.
misconceptions.why: A wing section isn't really half a Venturi nozzle, so the predicted velocity is wrong [S4].
misconceptions.truth: The velocity comes from the whole flow around the wing, which must conserve mass, momentum and energy together [S4].

misconceptions.myth: "Bernoulli" and "Newton" are rival explanations, and only one is right.
misconceptions.why: Integrating pressure around the body and integrating flow turning both give the same aerodynamic force [S4].
misconceptions.truth: Both are correct when applied properly; the arguments come from misapplying or over-simplifying them [S4].

tabs.title: Trade-offs
tabs.heading: Explanations compared
tabs.intro: For a science topic, 'trade-offs' means which explanation to reach for and where each one misleads.
useWhen: **Flow turning (Newton)**: explaining downwash, why angle of attack matters, and why there's no lift without air [S1]
**Pressure (Bernoulli)**: computing forces from a known velocity field around the wing [S4]
**Lift equation**: estimating how speed, area or air density change lift [S2]
avoidWhen: Using Bernoulli with an **assumed** speed, such as equal transit time or a Venturi shape [S4]
Using Newton on the **bottom surface only** (the skipping-stone picture) [S4]
Using the lift equation past the stall, where Cl changes rapidly with time [S3]
pros: Flow turning is intuitive and needs no equations
The pressure view connects directly to what wind-tunnel sensors measure
The lift equation packs every hard effect into one measured number, Cl [S2]
cons: Neither simple picture predicts the exact velocity distribution on its own [S4]
Cl has to be determined experimentally in general [S2]
Real lift also involves viscosity and compressibility, which these pictures leave out [S2]

perspectives.name: The 'Bernoulli' camp
perspectives.view: Lift comes from a pressure difference across the wing [S4].

perspectives.name: The 'Newton' camp
perspectives.view: Lift is the reaction force from deflecting a flow of gas [S4].

perspectives.name: NASA's view
perspectives.view: Both camps are correct: integrate pressure or integrate flow turning, and you get the same force [S4].

tabs.title: Cheatsheet
facts: Lift is a mechanical force: it needs a fluid and relative motion [S1]
Lift acts perpendicular to the flow, through the center of pressure [S1]
Lift ∝ V², so 2× speed gives 4× lift [S2]
Lift is roughly proportional to angle of attack within about ±10° for thin airfoils [S3]
A stall is boundary-layer separation at high angle of attack [S3]
Both Bernoulli and Newton are correct descriptions of lift [S4]

formulas.label: Dynamic pressure
formulas.note: The term shared by the lift equation and Bernoulli's equation [S2]

formulas.note: Static plus dynamic pressure is constant along the flow [S5]

quiz.q: According to NASA, what is the basic cause of lift?
options: A moving flow is turned by the wing
Air molecules meet at the trailing edge
Engines blow air over the wing's top
The wing is lighter than the air
quiz.why: Lift occurs when a moving flow of gas is turned by a solid object; the reaction pushes the wing the other way [S1].

quiz.q: A plane doubles its airspeed at the same angle and altitude. Roughly how does lift change?
options: It stays the same
It doubles
It quadruples
It halves

quiz.q: What is wrong with the 'equal transit time' explanation?
options: Bernoulli's equation is false for air
The top-surface speed it assumes is wrong
Wings have flat upper surfaces
Air underneath moves faster than above
quiz.why: Real flow over the top is much faster than equal transit predicts, so the assumed velocity, not Bernoulli, is the error [S4].

quiz.q: What happens to the flow when a wing stalls?
options: Air stops moving past the wing
Air speeds up under the wing
The engines stop producing thrust
The boundary layer separates on top
quiz.why: At high angles the boundary layer separates and the wing abruptly loses lift [S3].

quiz.q: Which statement about the 'Bernoulli' and 'Newton' explanations is correct?
options: Only the Newton picture is correct
Both give the same force if done right
Only the Bernoulli picture is correct
Neither one applies to real wings
quiz.why: Integrating pressure or flow turning around the body both determine the same aerodynamic force [S4].

quiz.q: A symmetric airfoil is set at 0° angle of attack. How much lift does it make?
options: None at all
The most possible
Exactly its weight
A small downforce
quiz.why: A symmetric airfoil makes zero lift at zero angle; a cambered one makes a little [S3].

quiz.q: Why don't the Space Shuttle's wings keep it in orbit?
options: They point the wrong way up
It flies too fast for wings
There's almost no air to turn
Its wings are too small
quiz.why: Lift needs contact with a fluid; space is nearly a vacuum, so the Shuttle stays up through orbital mechanics [S1].

options: Always straight up from the ground
Along the wing's chord line
Parallel to the oncoming flow
Perpendicular to the oncoming flow
quiz.why: Lift is the force component perpendicular to the flow direction [S1].
